focus_question: How does a fleet turn resources into useful work under communication, coordination, and failure constraints?
description: Follow the mechanisms that connect physical capacity, distributed execution, useful progress, serving contracts, and accountable operation. Draft relationships are bounded by their source evidence and conditions.
title: How does a fleet turn resources into useful work under communication, coordination, and failure constraints?

nodes.label: Distributed step time
nodes.summary: The critical-path time to advance one distributed training step, including compute, exposed communication, and coordination.
nodes.claim: Distributed step time is T_compute/N + T_comm(N) + T_sync(N) - T_overlap, so adding devices shrinks only the compute term while communication and synchronization persist, and scaling efficiency T_1/(N T_N) shows which term binds.

nodes.label: Communication intensity
nodes.summary: Network bytes transferred per unit of local computation for a specified distributed workload.
nodes.claim: Bytes moved across the network per local operation is the fleet analog of arithmetic intensity: below the fabric balance point scaling is easy, above it bisection bandwidth binds, and byte-reducing methods change it while overlap only hides exposed time.

nodes.label: Empirical scaling laws
nodes.teaches: Scaling laws as the demand curve
nodes.summary: Empirical relationships between model loss and training resources within a fitted regime.
nodes.claim: Loss falls as a power law toward an irreducible floor, so each equal quality gain multiplies the resource by a fixed factor, a predictable but sublinear return that keeps organizations buying each further order of magnitude of fleet.
nodes.concept: Scaling laws as the demand curve

nodes.label: Memory capacity
nodes.teaches: Capacity and bandwidth are separate tests
nodes.summary: The amount of state that can reside in a memory domain at once.
nodes.claim: Memory capacity decides whether model state fits and memory bandwidth decides how fast low-reuse phases run, so batch-1 decode is floored at weight bytes over HBM bandwidth and bandwidth per dollar becomes a procurement metric; the roofline and its ridge point (peak arithmetic over bandwidth) are the hardware screen that tells which ceiling a phase meets before any purchase.
nodes.concept: Capacity and bandwidth are separate tests

nodes.label: Bandwidth hierarchy
nodes.summary: The unequal data-transfer rates within an accelerator, within a node, and between nodes.
nodes.claim: Per-accelerator bandwidth falls roughly an order of magnitude at each physical boundary (HBM, NVLink, InfiniBand port, storage), so tensor parallelism stays in the fast domain, pipeline stages cross nodes, and data parallelism spans the cluster.

nodes.label: Rack power envelope
nodes.summary: The electrical and thermal limits on the equipment that a rack can operate concurrently.
nodes.claim: Accelerator TDP tripled across three generations while power density stopped shrinking, so watts per rack, delivery losses, cooling class, facility lead time, and synchronized current transients, not FLOP/s, bound installable compute.

nodes.label: Message startup latency
nodes.summary: The fixed startup component of a transfer that matters most for small messages.
nodes.claim: Point-to-point message time T(n) = alpha + n/beta splits at the crossover n* = alpha*beta, so small control and pipeline messages are startup-bound and barely gain from faster links while multi-MB gradient shards are bandwidth-bound.

nodes.label: Bisection bandwidth
nodes.summary: The minimum aggregate link capacity across any cut that divides the cluster into two equal groups.
nodes.claim: Traffic that crosses a cut is bounded by bisection bandwidth, so k:1 oversubscription multiplies the cut-crossing time by k, and fat-tree, torus, and dragonfly trade cut capacity against switches and cabling as a price-per-bisection-byte decision.

nodes.label: Network congestion
nodes.summary: Queueing and contention caused when offered traffic exceeds the service capacity of shared network paths.
nodes.claim: Under synchronized load end-to-end congestion control is a latency requirement, adaptive routing repairs ECMP collisions without adding capacity, and incast is spread in time, space, and priority rather than eliminated.

nodes.label: Input pipeline
nodes.summary: The staged path that reads, transforms, and delivers batches to accelerators.
nodes.claim: Required input bandwidth is the number of distinct consumers times target compute fraction times batch bytes over compute time, every stage of the chain must sustain it because delivered rate is the minimum over stages, and prefetch absorbs variance but never a sustained deficit; a direct DMA path from storage into accelerator memory (GPUDirect Storage, for example) removes the host-copy stage only when that copy is the limiting stage.

nodes.label: Prefetching
nodes.summary: Preparing future input batches while the current batch computes, subject to buffer and service-rate limits.
nodes.claim: Required input bandwidth is the number of distinct consumers times target compute fraction times batch bytes over compute time, every stage of the chain must sustain it because delivered rate is the minimum over stages, and prefetch absorbs variance but never a sustained deficit; a direct DMA path from storage into accelerator memory (GPUDirect Storage, for example) removes the host-copy stage only when that copy is the limiting stage.

nodes.label: Durable checkpoint
nodes.summary: A completed recoverable state version persisted beyond the failure domain it is meant to survive.
nodes.claim: A resumable mixed-precision Adam checkpoint is about 14 bytes per parameter, so a coordinated save must write each unique byte once, and tiered staging confines the exposed pause to the local write while the shared-tier copy drains in the background.

nodes.label: Versioned artifact
nodes.summary: An identifiable data or model version with a defined publication boundary and provenance.
nodes.claim: A fleet data pipeline is a DAG of immutable, content-identified artifacts that lets a run replay the exact batch behind a loss spike, and correctness under worker failure is decided at the output commit boundary by replayable inputs and idempotent writes; generated training data, which the data wall makes necessary, extends the contract with a provenance chain whose retained capacity and verification traffic are budgeted separately, and that lineage is what lets an investigation of model collapse trace the samples involved.

nodes.label: AllReduce
nodes.summary: A collective that reduces contributions from every participant and returns the result to every participant.
nodes.claim: A collective is a contract on what each rank holds afterward, not a schedule or a barrier: AllReduce = ReduceScatter + AllGather, AllToAll is a distributed transpose, and the right primitive is the narrowest one whose output the next computation consumes. Gradient synchronization, the AllReduce of the full gradient that every synchronous data-parallel step repeats, is defined here as the central case.

nodes.label: Communication overlap
nodes.summary: Executing eligible communication concurrently with independent compute to hide part of its elapsed cost.
nodes.claim: Gradient hooks launch each bucket's AllReduce as soon as it is ready so transfers hide under remaining backward work, but the last bucket is always exposed and a per-layer reduction slower than per-layer backward builds a backlog. LogP sets the limit by separating network latency, which independent work can hide, from processor overhead, which stays on the critical path.

nodes.label: Gradient compression
nodes.summary: Encoding gradient updates with fewer transmitted bits, with convergence and encoding costs to evaluate.
nodes.claim: Quantization and sparsification shrink only the byte term, biased compressors need an error-feedback residual to preserve cumulative gradient information, and compression pays only in time to target quality, not in bytes saved.

nodes.label: AllGather
nodes.summary: A collective that assembles the contributions of all ranks into a complete tensor at every rank.
nodes.claim: A collective is a contract on what each rank holds afterward, not a schedule or a barrier: AllReduce = ReduceScatter + AllGather, AllToAll is a distributed transpose, and the right primitive is the narrowest one whose output the next computation consumes. Gradient synchronization, the AllReduce of the full gradient that every synchronous data-parallel step repeats, is defined here as the central case.

nodes.label: ReduceScatter
nodes.summary: A collective that reduces corresponding input contributions and distributes different reduced shards among ranks.
nodes.claim: A collective is a contract on what each rank holds afterward, not a schedule or a barrier: AllReduce = ReduceScatter + AllGather, AllToAll is a distributed transpose, and the right primitive is the narrowest one whose output the next computation consumes. Gradient synchronization, the AllReduce of the full gradient that every synchronous data-parallel step repeats, is defined here as the central case.

nodes.label: Data parallelism
nodes.summary: Replicating a model across workers that process distinct portions of a batch and combine their updates.
nodes.claim: Replicated data parallelism reproduces the single-device global-batch update only when sampling, valid-item denominators, optimizer state, and update order match, and its price is one gradient AllReduce per step that throughput hides only while local compute covers it.

nodes.label: Tensor parallelism
nodes.teaches: Tensor parallelism in the fast domain
nodes.summary: Partitioning an individual layer's tensor computation across cooperating accelerators.
nodes.claim: Megatron tensor parallelism pays two activation AllReduces per transformer block on the critical path of every layer, so its degree is bounded by the fast intra-node domain.
nodes.concept: Tensor parallelism in the fast domain

nodes.label: Pipeline parallelism
nodes.summary: Partitioning model stages across devices and scheduling microbatches through those stages.
nodes.claim: Staging layers across devices moves only boundary activations point to point, but fill and drain idle each stage for (p-1)/(m+p-1) of the step, and 1F1B bounds retained activations so the many microbatches that shrink the bubble are affordable.

nodes.label: Training-state sharding
nodes.summary: Partitioning optimizer state, gradients, or parameters among data-parallel workers instead of keeping every state replicated.
nodes.claim: ZeRO and FSDP shard optimizer state, then gradients, then parameters, cutting per-device state from 16 bytes per parameter toward 16/N, while full parameter sharding raises traffic about 1.5x and puts parameter gathers on every layer's critical path.

nodes.label: Critical batch size
nodes.summary: A workload-dependent scale beyond which larger batches yield diminishing optimization progress per additional sample.
nodes.claim: Beyond the gradient-noise critical batch extra samples per step buy diminishing loss reduction, so the useful data-parallel width is about B_crit over the local batch, and learning-rate rules only extend the validated range.

nodes.label: Job failure rate
nodes.summary: The rate at which failures interrupt a specified distributed job under stated component and correlation assumptions.
nodes.claim: Independent constant-rate failures compose in series, so system MTBF = MTTF/N turns a 50,000-hour GPU into an interruption every few hours on a 10,000-GPU cluster, and correlated hazards over shared power, switches, and cooling come on top.

nodes.label: Consistent checkpoint cut
nodes.summary: A set of saved worker states that represents one mutually compatible point in distributed execution.
nodes.claim: A distributed checkpoint is recoverable only when its shards form a consistent cut and a manifest naming every shard is published last, so training uses coordinated checkpoints whose stage-then-publish protocol is a two-phase commit.

nodes.label: Recovery
nodes.summary: Detecting and isolating failure, restoring valid state, and returning the distributed job to useful execution.
nodes.claim: Each failure pays T_detect + T_restart + T_load + T_warmup on top of lost rework, which comes to dominate as clusters grow, and epochs, leases, and write fencing stop a stale worker from corrupting the recovered state.

nodes.label: Gang scheduling
nodes.summary: Allocating a tightly coupled job's required workers together so that partial allocation does not strand capacity.
nodes.claim: A rigid synchronous job makes no progress below its minimum gang, so partial allocation can deadlock two jobs at full cost, and atomic all-or-nothing allocation removes hold-and-wait but needs reservation, safe backfill, and holistic preemption.

nodes.label: Topology-aware placement
nodes.summary: Assigning a job's workers to physical resources according to its traffic pattern and available link hierarchy.
nodes.claim: Equal-size allocations deliver different throughput because bandwidth steps down from NVLink to leaf to spine, so placement minimizes a locality cost over the job's actual traffic, judged by completion time including the wait for a compact placement.

nodes.label: Resource fairness
nodes.summary: A selected rule for sharing feasible fleet capacity among competing users or jobs.
nodes.claim: A fair share of accelerators a job cannot run on delivers nothing, so the scheduler first filters feasible bundles (every resource dimension, gang atomicity, topology, memory) and only then applies dominant-resource fairness, while multi-dimensional packing strands capacity.

nodes.label: ML goodput
nodes.summary: The fraction of fleet capacity-time that becomes useful work at the hardware ideal rate, decomposed into scheduling, runtime, and program factors.
nodes.claim: Useful fleet output is capacity times scheduling, runtime, and program goodput, each counted on one accounting boundary so every lost hour is charged to exactly one factor.

nodes.label: Scheduling goodput
nodes.summary: The fraction of in-service fleet capacity-time held by complete allocations over a fixed calendar window; it does not measure work inside an allocation.
nodes.claim: Capacity counts only while held by a complete allocation, so partial gangs, fragmentation, and unmet demand are scheduling losses whose levers belong to orchestration.

nodes.label: Runtime goodput
nodes.summary: The fraction of allocated opportunity retained after execution interruptions and runtime overhead under the stated measurement contract.
nodes.claim: Allocated time counts only while it produces steps a checkpoint retains at the job's fault-free rate, so startup, input stalls, checkpoint pauses, restarts, and rework add up to the runtime loss.

nodes.label: Program goodput
nodes.summary: The fraction of the hardware ideal rate realized by useful program operations during retained execution; distinct from progress per training example.
nodes.claim: Program goodput measures retained step time against a named hardware ideal, reported as MFU against peak arithmetic (counting only the operations the model requires) or as MBU against the bandwidth floor for bandwidth-bound decode.

nodes.label: Statistical goodput
nodes.summary: Progress toward a specified learning target per processed training example, distinct from useful operations per second.
nodes.claim: Useful fleet output is capacity times scheduling, runtime, and program goodput, each counted on one accounting boundary so every lost hour is charged to exactly one factor.

nodes.label: SLO goodput
nodes.teaches: SLO goodput and the serving tax
nodes.summary: The rate of completed requests that meet the stated time-to-first-token (TTFT) and time-per-output-token (TPOT) targets for a fixed request mix.
nodes.claim: Serving capacity is the rate of completed requests that meet stated TTFT and per-token targets for a fixed mix, and end-to-end latency adds network, serialization, coordination, and queueing to model time, so a 70 ms model in a 100 ms budget leaves 30 ms for everything else.
nodes.concept: SLO goodput and the serving tax

nodes.label: Request batching
nodes.teaches: Batch formation trades waiting for reuse
nodes.summary: Grouping requests for shared accelerator execution to trade weight reuse against waiting time and resource demand.
nodes.claim: With batch service time t_0 + B t_req throughput saturates toward 1/t_req past a knee near t_0/t_req, and request latency is queueing plus formation plus execution, so a batching window caps formation but not queueing, while Little's law (in-flight work = arrival rate x mean latency) sizes the concurrency and replica count a target rate and latency imply.
nodes.concept: Batch formation trades waiting for reuse

nodes.label: KV cache
nodes.summary: Stored attention keys and values whose per-sequence growth constrains concurrent autoregressive requests.
nodes.claim: KV bytes per token = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dimension x bytes, so maximum batch is free HBM over context times bytes per token, weight fit does not establish serving capacity, and each lever changes a different factor; resident LoRA adapters draw on the same HBM pool, so adapter locality is an admission decision, and preempting a running request means choosing to retain, swap, recompute, or reject its KV state against the waiting request's deadline.

nodes.label: Resident sequence count
nodes.summary: The number of active sequences whose attention state resides in a serving replica; feasible count depends on their total cached tokens and available memory.
nodes.claim: KV bytes per token = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dimension x bytes, so maximum batch is free HBM over context times bytes per token, weight fit does not establish serving capacity, and each lever changes a different factor; resident LoRA adapters draw on the same HBM pool, so adapter locality is an admission decision, and preempting a running request means choosing to retain, swap, recompute, or reject its KV state against the waiting request's deadline.

nodes.label: Federated averaging
nodes.teaches: FedAvg under sampling and non-IID data
nodes.summary: Combining client-trained model updates into a shared model using an explicitly defined weighting rule.
nodes.claim: FedAvg is local SGD under a sampled cohort and non-IID shards, so local epochs that save uplink rounds also pull clients toward their own optima (client drift), and the comparison is measured time to a quality target, not rounds.
nodes.concept: FedAvg under sampling and non-IID data

nodes.label: Client participation
nodes.summary: The selected set and sampling process of devices that contribute to a federated round.
nodes.claim: Passing the device admission test correlates with hardware, charging habits, and connectivity, so the federated model learns from the admitted population rather than the deployed one, and over-selection with a round deadline concentrates that bias; the skew is sized per cohort as a coverage ratio, the cohort's share of completed updates over its share of the deployed population.

nodes.label: Secure aggregation
nodes.summary: A protocol that reveals an aggregate update while hiding individual contributions within its stated threat model.
nodes.claim: Data locality is not privacy, because updates and metadata still leak, so secure aggregation's cancelling pairwise masks hide each client's update from the coordinator at the cost of a participation floor (a secret-sharing threshold of survivors, and enough clients that the sum hides each one) and dropout recovery (survivors' shares rebuild a dropped client's masks in an extra round), while differential privacy bounds a different boundary.

nodes.label: Evaluation contract
nodes.summary: The versioned definition of a deployment's task, evidence, acceptance tests, and operating limits.
nodes.claim: A fleet release is accepted against one versioned record that pins, for the same artifact, offline, system, responsibility, online, and recovery evidence, each with an owner and an invalidation rule fixed before exposure.

nodes.label: Staged rollout
nodes.summary: Incrementally exposing live traffic to a candidate release while measuring acceptance and preserving rollback capability.
nodes.claim: Rollout risk is probability of regression times per-unit impact times exposed units, so a canary stage lasts at least its planned sample over traffic share, and the slowest outcome the release must observe sets the schedule.

nodes.label: Dependency registry
nodes.summary: A versioned record of model artifacts, provenance, evaluations, and dependencies used for impact analysis and release control.
nodes.claim: Per-model validation does not establish compatibility along a chain, so the registry records upstream and downstream edges whose traversal yields the impact set, and a release names a compatible version set whose rollback unit may span a pipeline.

nodes.label: Data poisoning
nodes.summary: Adversarial manipulation of training data or updates to alter learned behavior.
nodes.claim: A poisoner needs write access to something the model learns from and solves a bilevel problem over the defender's training, so targeted, backdoor, and subpopulation attacks can leave aggregate validation accuracy unchanged, and clean-label poisons that keep every label correct pass any label audit, as concept poisoning of a text-to-image model (Nightshade) shows at a dose of a few hundred images.

nodes.label: Differential privacy
nodes.summary: A mechanism-level bound on how much a released-result distribution changes when a specified protected contribution changes.
nodes.claim: (epsilon, delta)-differential privacy bounds how much one protected unit can change a release, named by an adjacency relation, so it holds against any auxiliary information, and noise scaled to sensitivity over epsilon costs small groups the most.

nodes.label: Privacy budget
nodes.summary: The accumulated privacy-loss guarantee for a declared neighboring relation, sampling process, and composition rule.
nodes.claim: Privacy loss accumulates across every data-dependent release about the same population, so DP-SGD's many sampled steps need a tested accountant whose recorded inputs (sampling, noise, steps, clipping, adjacency) form the release record, and the cumulative budget becomes a release gate.

nodes.label: Distribution shift
nodes.summary: A change between training or reference data and the operational data-generating distribution.
nodes.claim: Covariate shift changes P(x), label shift changes P(y), and concept drift changes P(y|x), so input monitors can be silent under pure concept drift and the type of shift selects the remedy (reweighting, recalibration, or adaptation on fresh labels).

nodes.label: Selective prediction
nodes.summary: A decision rule that answers selected requests and abstains or routes the remainder under a measured risk-coverage contract.
nodes.claim: Population monitors cannot say whether one request lies inside demonstrated competence, so serving trades coverage against selective risk along a threshold, and conformal prediction adds a coverage guarantee that holds only under exchangeability.

nodes.label: Poisoning defenses
nodes.summary: Layered controls on source provenance, incoming data, training, and post-training behavior that reduce specified poisoning risks.
nodes.claim: Because poisoned records can preserve clean aggregate accuracy, defense runs as ordered layers along the data path (ingress controls, anomaly detection and sanitization, robust training, post-training checks), each with a named blind spot, made reversible by lineage.

nodes.label: Fallback capacity
nodes.summary: The service or human-review capacity needed to handle the rate and work of requests deferred by the primary predictor within their response deadlines.
nodes.claim: Population monitors cannot say whether one request lies inside demonstrated competence, so serving trades coverage against selective risk along a threshold, and conformal prediction adds a coverage guarantee that holds only under exchangeability.

nodes.label: Operational carbon
nodes.summary: Emissions attributed to operating energy under a stated facility boundary and grid-carbon signal.
nodes.claim: Operational CO2 = IT energy x PUE x grid carbon intensity, three terms acting at separate tiers, and PUE measures only non-IT overhead, so a coal-fed site can beat a hydro-fed one on PUE.

nodes.label: Embodied carbon
nodes.summary: Emissions from manufacturing and other non-operating lifecycle processes allocated to the measured system or workload.
nodes.claim: Manufacturing emissions are fixed before first power-on and allocated to work by a declared rule, so their share of a job's footprint rises on clean grids and at low utilization and decides when replacing hardware pays.

nodes.label: Carbon-aware scheduling
nodes.summary: Choosing workload time or location using a declared carbon signal while respecting deadlines, capacity, and movement costs.
nodes.claim: Moving work to cleaner regions or hours changes the emissions factor, not the energy, so it must use a marginal signal from a forecast, meet deadline, data, capacity, and reliability constraints, and beat the cost of the move.

nodes.label: Operating energy
nodes.summary: The time integral of operating power across a declared set of devices and facility consumers.
nodes.claim: A facility cannot draw more than its grid feed and cooling capacity at any instant, while run energy integrates average power over time, so a short run can be infeasible at modest energy and a long run feasible at large energy.

nodes.label: Assurance case
nodes.summary: A bounded deployment claim supported by evidence, controls, accountable ownership, and rules for material change.
nodes.claim: A registry proves which weights shipped, not that shipping was justified, so deployment is justified by a versioned assurance case (claim for a stated use, argument, evidence, assumptions, an owner who can block, an invalidation rule) that expires on material change and maps the applicable legal obligations onto the lifecycle.

nodes.label: Fairness criterion
nodes.summary: A selected formal or normative requirement about how model outcomes or errors are distributed across affected groups.
nodes.claim: Demographic parity, equalized odds, equality of opportunity, and calibration measure different conditional rates, one classifier can fail all of them at once, and they cannot all hold when base rates differ, so choosing one is a governance decision.

nodes.label: Contestability
nodes.summary: The ability of affected people to challenge a decision and obtain investigation and an actionable remedy.
nodes.claim: Explanation serves accountability only when an affected person can challenge a decision and obtain correction, which requires decision provenance, audience-appropriate reasons, an appeal routed to an authorized reviewer, and tracked outcomes.

edges.explanation: Scaling model parameters increases the memory required before a training run can begin.
edges.conditions: Within the fitted scaling regime and specified model precision.

evidence.quote: The scaling laws of @sec-vol2-intro-ai-scaling-laws-a043 are why demand outruns any single device. Loss falls predictably as parameters, training tokens, and compute grow together, so each step up in capability multiplies both the memory a model occupies and the arithmetic its training consumes; a GPT-3-class model already needs several accelerators merely to store its FP16 weights. A model that exceeds one accelerator's memory capacity forces a hardware decision before training begins. Adding accelerators supplies capacity, but also creates transfers between devices, increases power demand, and couples progress to more components that can fail. The familiar single-node compute and memory limits therefore become inputs to fleet design. Four recurring physical constraints appear at escalating physical scales, from an eight-GPU node to a 25K-accelerator fleet (@fig-three-walls-grid). Memory bandwidth, rack power, pod communication, and fleet failure exposure provide the examples; the workload and configuration determine which constraint binds at each scale. These are the memory, energy, and network walls of the scale moment and the fleet's reliability gap, seen from the hardware that imposes them. Because this chapter studies the hardware, it names each constraint by the physical resource that runs out. It uses these four names from here on: the memory wall, the power wall (the energy wall as power delivery and heat removal), the communication wall (the network wall as link bandwidth), and the reliability wall (the reliability gap as a failure interval).

edges.label: drive demand for

edges.explanation: More network bytes per local operation make communication harder to hide and can make the fabric the binding constraint.
edges.conditions: At fixed fabric capability; overlap depends on independent compute.

evidence.quote: *Past the fabric balance point, step time grows with communication intensity.*

edges.label: increases exposed cost in

edges.explanation: Sharding reduces state replicated on each accelerator so larger training jobs can fit.
edges.conditions: State sharding incurs communication and implementation costs.

evidence.quote: ***Sharded data parallelism***\index{Sharded data parallelism!definition}\index{ZeRO!definition} partitions optimizer state, gradients, and at the deepest stage the parameters themselves across data-parallel workers. Each worker processes its own minibatch shard and uses collectives to obtain the parameters and reduced gradients it needs. Full sharding reduces each worker's persistent state toward $1/\DeviceCount$ of the replicated training state; activations and temporary buffers still contribute to peak memory.

edges.label: motivates

edges.explanation: Frequent tensor-parallel exchanges belong in the fast interconnect domain.
edges.conditions: Placement must reflect the actual traffic pattern and measured link capacity.

evidence.quote: **Systems insight**: For the same payload, the example inter-node path has a transfer-time lower bound `{python} BandwidthStaircase.bs_gap_nv_ib_mult_str` larger than the example intra-node path. Size alone does not decide which traffic may cross that cliff; frequency and overlap do. Tensor parallelism\index{Tensor parallelism!intra-node} exchanges activations inside every layer, on the critical path, so it favors the fast local NVLink domain in this configuration. Data parallelism\index{Data parallelism!inter-node} moves the largest buffer, the full gradient, but only once per step and overlapped with the backward pass, so it can cross the scarce InfiniBand tier. A partition that fits in memory can still spend much of a step waiting if its exposed exchanges exceed the communication budget.

edges.label: constrains

edges.explanation: A placement must fit the power and heat-removal capacity of its physical domain.
edges.conditions: Power and cooling are feasibility constraints, not merely average energy costs.

evidence.quote: Every floating-point operation dissipates energy as heat. Dense Tensor Core activity during large matrix multiplications drives heat proportional to the switching activity of billions of transistors. Fleet design must pair each accelerator's sustained power envelope with any documented transient excursion requirement. At dense fleet scale, this produces the power wall\index{Power wall!facility constraint}, the point at which facility power delivery and heat removal, rather than available arithmetic units, determine how much compute can be installed and sustained.

edges.label: bounds feasible

edges.explanation: Collective latency depends on the number of communication rounds as well as transferred bytes.
edges.conditions: Alpha-beta approximations require calibration for the backend and message regime.

evidence.quote: The $\MessageStartupLatency$-$\LinkBandwidth$ model\index{Hockney model!latency and bandwidth} $\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth$ prices a transfer over a single link (principle \ref{pri-alpha-beta-model}), separating a fixed startup cost ($\MessageStartupLatency$) from a per-byte transfer cost ($\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth$) [@hockney1994]. A collective pays that price at every step of its schedule, so the two terms, multiplied by the schedule's round count and traffic factor, determine algorithm selection across the fleet.

edges.label: adds per-round cost to

edges.explanation: Global collective traffic must cross the provisioned network cuts.
edges.conditions: Applies to the collective participant group and its actual communication schedule.

evidence.quote: ***Bisection bandwidth***\index{Bisection bandwidth!definition} is a network topology metric defined as the minimum aggregate link capacity crossing any partition that divides the cluster into two equal halves, representing the worst-case throughput ceiling for traffic that must cross that partition, including global collectives.

edges.label: bounds cross-cut traffic for

edges.explanation: Contended paths can delay the shared exchange and its synchronization boundary.
edges.conditions: The effect depends on traffic placement and the job critical path.

evidence.quote: The flow inversion compounds this problem. Traditional networks are designed for fairness among millions of "mice flows,"\index{Mice flow!network traffic}[^fn-elephant-flow-collision] yet ML training is dominated by a few "elephant flows"\index{Elephant flow!gradient AllReduce} corresponding to the gradient AllReduce. The full 175B model has `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.grad_gb_str` of gradient state at the assumed precision, but a sharded job distributes that state across workers. Each collective operates on its participating group and local payload; its algorithm determines how much each worker sends. Standard flow control and routing mechanisms like equal-cost multi-path (ECMP)\index{ECMP!elephant flow limitations}\index{Multi-path routing|see{ECMP}}\index{Equal-cost multi-path|see{ECMP}}, which hash each flow onto one of several equal-cost paths, are poorly suited to this traffic pattern. A static hash\index{ECMP!hash polarization} cannot subdivide one elephant flow across all available links, and it can inadvertently map multiple elephant flows to the same link, creating massive congestion while other links sit idle.

edges.label: can lengthen

edges.explanation: Preparing batches ahead can overlap input work with accelerator execution.
edges.conditions: Buffers must fit and long-run producer service rate must meet consumer demand.

evidence.quote: Pipelining converts a sequential bottleneck into overlapped execution (@fig-data-pipeline-vol2), but continuous saturation requires a prefetch buffer deep enough to absorb variance in I/O latency. Stage durations need not be deterministic if ready batches cover the delays. Storage systems experience I/O jitter\index{I/O jitter!sources and pipeline impact}: variation in read latency caused by contention and background work. NVMe drives suffer occasional latency spikes during internal garbage collection (when the controller reorganizes NAND flash blocks) or wear-leveling operations. Parallel file systems incur spikes when multiple training jobs contend for the same OSS nodes, when the MDS processes a burst of metadata operations, or when background scrubbing detects and repairs bit errors. Object storage likewise exposes delays from shared-service contention and maintenance.

edges.label: hides latency in

edges.explanation: Late input delivery leaves accelerators idle and delays useful progress.
edges.conditions: Input stalls matter only when input service lies on the execution critical path.

evidence.quote: **Systems insight**: Even with pipelining, the accelerator is idle `{python} PipelineCalcs.data_stall_pct_str` of the time. To eliminate the stall entirely, the next batch must arrive within the `{python} PipelineCalcs.t_comp_stall_str` compute window, either by increasing effective storage bandwidth or by adding parallel I/O streams. Deeper prefetch buffers cannot help here, because the delivery time exceeds the compute window on every step rather than merely in the tail.

edges.label: can lengthen

edges.explanation: A saved state protects progress only when its committed copy survives the relevant failure.
edges.conditions: The checkpoint must be complete, discoverable, and outside the failed domain.

evidence.quote: Asynchronous checkpointing shrinks even that local-flash pause by staging the snapshot in host DRAM first. Nodes coordinate the training step to capture, copy each accelerator-resident shard into a dedicated pinned host-memory buffer, and resume training immediately while a background thread writes the buffer to local NVMe. The snapshot buffer must remain immutable until the background write finishes; separate live-state buffers allow training to advance without changing the captured generation. If a node fails during the asynchronous write, its local shard may be incomplete. The job must wait for the required writes or peer replication before declaring this generation durable, even if training has already resumed.

edges.label: provides restore state for

edges.explanation: Registry records identify artifacts and their provenance for dependency and release decisions.
edges.conditions: Identity and provenance do not by themselves establish behavioral correctness.

evidence.quote: Without explicit dependency tracking, organizations discover architectural coupling through production outages when an upstream change silently corrupts downstream assumptions. A single YAML entry captures artifact location, training provenance, evaluation results, and declared dependencies (@lst-registry-schema). The downstream entries seed impact analysis; following their registry records reveals transitive consumers. Release approval additionally requires confirming that the update preserves the input-output contract expected by those consumers, or scheduling a coordinated rollout while retaining a validated rollback target.

edges.label: preserves provenance for

edges.explanation: Data-parallel workers use reduction to combine gradient contributions.
edges.conditions: Participants must agree on tensor layout, ordering, weighting, and completion semantics.

evidence.quote: Parameter updating closes the replicated synchronous contract. After the gradient AllReduce [@patarasuk2009], every worker holds the same global gradient and applies it to its own replica with SGD, momentum, or Adam\index{Adam!distributed update}, so the update stays decentralized without losing equivalence to single-device training. Identical gradients alone are insufficient, because optimizer moments, learning rates, and step counts must also match across replicas. Frameworks automate the cycle of splitting data, computing gradients, synchronizing, and updating, but they cannot remove the ordering constraint that keeps the replicas coherent: every worker must finish aggregating the current step's gradient before any replica computes from the updated weights.

edges.label: combines gradients in

edges.explanation: Overlap can shorten the critical path without reducing the number of bytes moved.
edges.conditions: Only communication concurrent with independent useful compute can be hidden.

evidence.quote: The pipeline also has boundary effects\index{Communication-computation overlap!boundary effects}. During the first backward computation, no gradient from this pass is ready to communicate. Once the output-side gradient is ready, however, its communication can overlap with the remaining backward work. At the other end, the input-side gradient has no subsequent backward computation to hide its transfer. More layers create a longer overlap window, but depth alone does not guarantee high coverage: if communication takes longer than each compute interval, a backlog remains even in a deep model.

edges.label: reduces exposed time in

edges.explanation: Compression changes transmitted bytes at the cost of encoding work and possible convergence effects.
edges.conditions: Compare time to target quality, including error feedback and encoding overhead.

evidence.quote: Training across data centers over wide-area links or on cloud instances with commodity Ethernet can leave each worker with 10--100$\times$ less network bandwidth than the reference InfiniBand fabric. Federated training on phone-class devices, the Archetype C (Federated MobileNet) regime, faces cellular or Wi-Fi uplinks that are both slower and intermittently available. Even after hierarchical routing and schedule tuning extract all usable capacity from such links, moving a full-precision gradient or a multi-step client update can still dominate step time. Gradient compression attacks the payload size directly by trading numerical representation fidelity for fewer transmitted bits, offering nominal value-payload reductions of 4--1000$\times$ before metadata and aggregation costs reduce the realized savings. Because noisy or biased updates can slow or stall optimization, the central engineering question is how much communication volume a compressor can remove while preserving progress toward the training quality target.

edges.label: reduces

edges.explanation: Pipeline fill and drain can leave stages idle and reduce achieved parallel efficiency.
edges.conditions: Bubble cost depends on stages, microbatch count, schedule, and activation storage.

evidence.quote:
**Math**:
For balanced, noninterleaved synchronous stages under the one-forward-one-backward (1F1B) schedule developed below, with ideal transfers, the bubble fraction follows from the stage and microbatch counts. The time units below each combine one forward and one backward service interval; they are not individual optimizer steps.

edges.label: adds bubbles to

edges.explanation: Full sharding partitions persistent model state among workers, while activations and temporary buffers still contribute to peak memory.
edges.conditions: Capacity savings must include peak gathers, activation storage, and communication costs.

evidence.quote: ***Sharded data parallelism***\index{Sharded data parallelism!definition}\index{ZeRO!definition} partitions optimizer state, gradients, and at the deepest stage the parameters themselves across data-parallel workers. Each worker processes its own minibatch shard and uses collectives to obtain the parameters and reduced gradients it needs. Full sharding reduces each worker's persistent state toward $1/\DeviceCount$ of the replicated training state; activations and temporary buffers still contribute to peak memory.

edges.label: reduces per-worker demand on

edges.explanation: More frequent interruptions change the balance between checkpoint overhead and lost work.
edges.conditions: Independent-failure approximations require adjustment for correlated failures and varying checkpoint cost.

evidence.quote: Setting the first derivative to zero ($\frac{d\CheckpointWasteFraction}{d\CheckpointInterval} = -\frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval^2} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot \SystemMtbf} = 0$) directly yields the square-root minimum of @eq-ft-young-daly-interval. As clusters grow, system MTBF drops, so the optimal interval shrinks, demanding higher-bandwidth storage to keep $\CheckpointWriteTime$ small before checkpoint overhead consumes the cluster's compute capacity. Because the relationship is a square root, halving MTBF tightens the interval by only $\sqrt{2}\approx 1.4\times$, so doubling cluster size does not demand doubling checkpoint I/O bandwidth when checkpoint size and the other assumptions stay fixed. Substituting the optimum back into @eq-ft-checkpoint-waste gives a minimum waste of $\sqrt{2\CheckpointWriteTime/\SystemMtbf}$. Because $\SystemMtbf$ falls as $1/\DeviceCount$ under independent failures, that optimized overhead grows as $\sqrt{\DeviceCount}$, and doubling the cluster raises it by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$ even though the interval itself adapts.

edges.label: raises demand for

edges.explanation: Recovery must restore mutually compatible worker states rather than arbitrary local snapshots.
edges.conditions: The cut must cover optimizer, model, and execution state required by the training contract.

evidence.quote: If workers in a sharded training job save their local shards at different steps without coordinating, rolling one failed worker back to its last save invalidates every peer that already consumed gradients or activations from its later steps. Rollbacks then cascade backward through the run in the classic domino effect [@elnozahy2002survey]. Avoiding that cascade requires choosing how workers coordinate across two orthogonal dimensions. Workers can vary in whether they synchronize to capture a consistent cut (**coordinated** versus **uncoordinated checkpointing**\index{Checkpointing!uncoordinated}\index{Uncoordinated checkpointing|see{Checkpointing}}). They can also vary in whether they funnel state through one writer or persist shards in parallel (centralized versus distributed checkpointing). Because distributed ML workers exchange state at every step, production training relies on **coordinated checkpointing**\index{Checkpointing!coordinated}\index{Coordinated checkpointing|see{Checkpointing}}. In this scheme, workers synchronize at step boundaries or through an explicit two-phase commit protocol, so that all saved shards belong to a single globally consistent recovery line. Once coordination guarantees consistency, the remaining architectural decision is how those shards reach persistent storage: whether workers funnel their state through a single coordinator or write their partitions directly in parallel.

edges.label: is required for correct

edges.explanation: Time spent restoring execution reduces the useful fraction of allocated opportunity.
edges.conditions: Use the runtime-goodput accounting window; checkpoint cost and failure loss must not be double counted.

evidence.quote:
- *Startup* spans the interval from gang completion to the first training step while processes launch, libraries load, collective communicators initialize, checkpoint weights load, and compilers warm up. Because scheduler logs timestamp gang completion and the job timeline timestamps the first step, startup is measured directly between those two records—which is why @sec-performance-engineering-scheduling-evidence requires the scheduler, rather than the first step, to mark allocation completion.
- *Input waits* capture the time a retained step spends blocked on the data pipeline for its next batch, carved out of step duration per @sec-performance-engineering-goodput-boundaries.
- *Synchronous checkpoint pauses* capture the intervals during which training halts while accelerators or hosts flush state to persistent storage.
- *Failure recovery and rework* cover both the downtime from a fault through detection, relaunch, state reload, and warmup, and the held time spent earlier on post-checkpoint steps that the failure erased and the job had to repeat.
- *Forced preemption and planned reconfiguration* charge the post-checkpoint work discarded by an eviction, the subsequent reload after readmission, and the warmup before steady-state step times return, along with planned maintenance drains or elastic resizes. All of these belong to runtime goodput because the job held a complete allocation while the discarded or non-step hours were spent.

edges.label: reduces

edges.explanation: Tightly coupled synchronous jobs require their worker set to be available together.
edges.conditions: The job may combine data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism; a gang is not exclusive to data parallelism.

evidence.quote: Partial allocation of rigid multi-GPU jobs creates a distributed scheduling failure mode in which two jobs each hold half the resources they need and block each other indefinitely while every allocated GPU sits idle. In the left panel of @fig-gang-scheduling-deadlock, jobs J1 and J2 each hold 4 of the 8 GPUs they require, and the whole pool stalls. Atomic gang scheduling\index{Gang scheduling!atomic allocation} (right panel) instead grants J1 all 8 GPUs as one allocation while J2 waits without holding any, which prevents this allocation deadlock.

edges.label: admits workers together for

edges.explanation: Topology-aware placement keeps the most communication-intensive groups within fast physical domains.
edges.conditions: Feasible placements must also satisfy capacity, power, and isolation requirements.

evidence.quote: A **hierarchical placement**\index{Hierarchical placement!definition} algorithm applies these constraints from the most restrictive communication domain outward, matching each 3D parallelism dimension to the interconnect tier its traffic can tolerate (@fig-fleet-orchestration-hierarchical-placement). In the illustrated fleet, it places each tensor-parallel group within an NVLink-connected node, where the per-layer activation exchanges run at `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.nvlink_h100_perdir_gb_per_s_str`. It places consecutive pipeline stages under the same leaf switch, where stage boundaries cross at `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str`. It distributes data-parallel replicas across racks only when the once-per-step gradient synchronization fits the roughly `{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_lo_num_str`--`{python} FleetTopologyInterconnect.oversub_hi_gb_per_s_str` per endpoint that an oversubscribed spine leaves. This alignment reduces costly boundary crossings, but placement alone cannot reserve the fabric's full bisection bandwidth against other jobs.

edges.label: matches traffic to

edges.explanation: Fair sharing chooses among allocations that can actually execute the job.
edges.conditions: The fairness objective and resource-accounting boundary must be declared.

evidence.quote: Awarding the 64-GPU fine-tuning run its fair share of the cluster delivers zero progress if those GPUs sit on nodes with exhausted host memory, lack the interconnect its parallel layout requires, or arrive only 32 at a time. A scheduling objective can choose only among allocations that a job can actually run. Fairness must be computed across every resource a tenant consumes, a request must fit every dimension of the node that receives it, a rigid group must arrive whole, and the resources each job holds must not block one another. Each of these constraints narrows the feasible set before any objective selects within it.

edges.label: is applied after feasible

edges.explanation: Waiting for a complete worker set changes how much fleet opportunity reaches the workload.
edges.conditions: Evaluate allocation efficiency and waiting time over the same measurement window.

evidence.quote: A rigid distributed training job holding half of its requested accelerators while waiting for the rest completes zero steps, not half as many, yet a naive utilization counter credits every assigned device as busy. Scheduling goodput eliminates that distortion by taking the ratio of two capacity-time integrals over the same calendar window. The denominator is the in-service capacity-time offered by the pool: its allocatable accelerators multiplied by the window duration. The numerator is the all-allocated capacity-time held by complete allocations, summed across jobs as each job's device count multiplied by the interval from the moment its minimum gang became complete until release. A complete allocation corresponds to the minimum viable execution group of @sec-fleet-orchestration-gang-scheduling—every accelerator, interconnect domain, and co-scheduled host resource required to execute one synchronous step. For a rigid job, that group is the full requested gang; for an elastic job, it is the active gang size between two reconfiguration boundaries, and any accelerators the job relinquishes re-enter the numerator only when another complete allocation claims them. Because nothing inside the allocation enters this ratio, a wedged job that holds a complete gang without running a step achieves the same scheduling goodput as a job executing at peak FLOP/s.

evidence.quote: ***ML productivity goodput (MPG)***\index{ML productivity goodput!definition}\index{Goodput!definition} is the fraction of a fleet's capacity-time that becomes useful work at the hardware's ideal rate, expressed as the product of scheduling, runtime, and program goodput, each measured on a fixed accounting boundary so that every lost interval is charged to exactly one factor [@wongpanich2025fleet].

edges.conditions: Do not substitute accelerator peak utilization for useful progress toward a quality target.

evidence.quote: ***ML productivity goodput (MPG)***\index{ML productivity goodput!definition}\index{Goodput!definition} is the fraction of a fleet's capacity-time that becomes useful work at the hardware's ideal rate, expressed as the product of scheduling, runtime, and program goodput, each measured on a fixed accounting boundary so that every lost interval is charged to exactly one factor [@wongpanich2025fleet].

edges.label: is a factor in

edges.explanation: Batching improves reuse but can make requests miss the serving latency contract.
edges.conditions: A batch policy must be evaluated at the specified arrival process and latency percentile.

evidence.quote: Processing multiple requests together shares weight reads and kernel launch overhead across more useful work. The resulting service-rate gain can reduce queueing, but waiting to form a batch adds delay; the net effect on request latency depends on load. Single-machine serving applies this insight through dynamic batching\index{Dynamic batching}, which collects requests within a time window before processing them together.

edges.label: trades waiting against

edges.explanation: Growing per-request KV state constrains how many active sequences can share a replica.
edges.conditions: Capacity depends on model, precision, sequence lengths, allocator behavior, and reserved headroom.

evidence.quote: A replica's KV footprint is that cost multiplied by every token it holds, $\KvCacheMemory = \BatchSize \times \SequenceLength \times \KvCacheBytesPerToken$, so the largest admissible batch at context $\SequenceLength$ is the HBM left after weights and runtime allocations divided by $\SequenceLength \times \KvCacheBytesPerToken$. Each serving lever acts on a different factor. Grouped-query attention lowers $\KvHeadCount$, KV quantization lowers $\ElementStorageSize$, a shorter admitted context lowers $\SequenceLength$, and paging returns HBM lost to fragmentation without changing the per-token cost. The notebook below turns this budget into an explicit batch-size limit for a production node.

edges.label: bounds

edges.explanation: Serving useful work counts only output satisfying the declared serving contract.
edges.conditions: Do not equate raw token throughput with deadline-qualified useful output or training progress.

evidence.quote: The same targets also define the serving system's capacity metric. **SLO goodput**\index{Goodput!SLO-constrained} is the rate of completed requests that meet the stated TTFT and TPOT targets for a fixed request mix. It is the serving counterpart of the useful-progress goodput that coordination protects in training (@sec-vol2-introduction-dim-coord), and it applies after ML goodput, which measures how much of a replica's held capacity runs at its ideal rate. SLO goodput then counts how much of that capacity completes requests within their targets. A request that misses its contract counts for nothing, however busy the accelerators were while serving it, so increasing arrivals without completing more requests within those targets does not increase useful capacity.

edges.label: uses a different contract from

edges.explanation: Client availability and selection determine which data distributions influence the aggregate update.
edges.conditions: Weights and sampling corrections must match the intended population objective.

evidence.quote: Scheduling must therefore balance completion speed with population coverage. Stratified or quota-based sampling can prioritize underrepresented groups among eligible devices, while cumulative participation records can guide later invitations. Weighting methods require estimates of the population and selection process; they cannot recover observations from a cohort that never participates. Buffered asynchronous aggregation [@fedbuff], whose mechanism @sec-edge-intelligence-asynchronous-device-synchronization-348e describes, staleness-aware methods [@rodio2024], and fairness-oriented weighting [@fedstaleweight] offer additional controls. Their effectiveness must be checked through completed participation and cohort quality, rather than inferred from the scheduling rule alone. Example weighting in the aggregate (@eq-fedavg-weighted-aggregation) also gives large local datasets more influence whether or not they represent the target population any better.

edges.label: changes the sample used by

edges.explanation: Secure aggregation restricts visibility of client contributions while exposing an aggregate.
edges.conditions: The guarantee is bounded by cohort size, dropouts, collusion, and the protocol threat model.

evidence.quote: Secure aggregation also creates a robustness conflict. Byzantine-resilient rules\index{Secure aggregation!Byzantine resilience conflict} such as Krum, coordinate-wise filtering, or per-client anomaly inspection need access to individual updates, while secure aggregation deliberately hides those updates [@blanchard2017machine; @bonawitz2017]. A system cannot claim both arbitrary per-client inspection and conventional secure aggregation over the same messages. It must instead validate clients before masking, use attested execution and bounded local updates, compute only aggregation-compatible checks, or adopt a protocol designed to evaluate approved robust statistics without revealing raw client contributions. @Fig-secure-agg models this cryptographic boundary through pairwise zero-sum masking. Clients A and B negotiate a shared random mask $\PairwiseMaskSecret$ via Diffie-Hellman key agreement. They perturb their local updates into pseudo-random vectors ($\FirstClientMaskedUpdate = \FiniteChange\FirstClientModelParameters+ \PairwiseMaskSecret$ and $\SecondClientMaskedUpdate = \FiniteChange\SecondClientModelParameters- \PairwiseMaskSecret$) before crossing into the server domain. When the aggregation server sums the received vectors, the symmetric masks cancel ($\PairwiseMaskSecret - \PairwiseMaskSecret = 0$), yielding the exact unmasked aggregate $\FiniteChange\FirstClientModelParameters+ \FiniteChange\SecondClientModelParameters$. This two-client illustration assumes both clients complete the exchange and neither reveals its mask to the server. It demonstrates cancellation, not a complete protocol for collusion resistance or dropout recovery.

edges.label: hides individual inputs to

edges.explanation: Hiding individual update messages does not alone bound information leakage through the released aggregate or model.
edges.conditions: Secure aggregation and differential privacy protect against different observers and disclosures.

evidence.quote: Secure aggregation and differential privacy\index{Differential privacy!composition with secure aggregation} can protect different boundaries, but their composition must follow the threat model. If a trusted server adds noise after receiving an exact aggregate, the privacy guarantee applies to the released noisy result; it does not hide that exact aggregate from the server. A protocol designed for distributed noise can instead let the server receive only a noisy aggregate. Clipping, noise calibration, dropout assumptions, and repeated-release accounting must match the chosen protocol. Neither mechanism establishes that local data or updates are trustworthy.

edges.label: does not substitute for

edges.explanation: Recorded consumers support impact analysis, compatible release ordering, and validated rollback targets.
edges.conditions: Registry entries must be current and compatibility must be tested rather than inferred from a link.

evidence.quote: Without explicit dependency tracking, organizations discover architectural coupling through production outages when an upstream change silently corrupts downstream assumptions. A single YAML entry captures artifact location, training provenance, evaluation results, and declared dependencies (@lst-registry-schema). The downstream entries seed impact analysis; following their registry records reveals transitive consumers. Release approval additionally requires confirming that the update preserves the input-output contract expected by those consumers, or scheduling a coordinated rollout while retaining a validated rollback target.

edges.label: enables dependency checks for

edges.explanation: Rollout acceptance must evaluate the actual deployed pipeline against a versioned task and evidence contract.
edges.conditions: Offline model accuracy alone does not establish the deployed service contract.

evidence.quote: Shadow runs, experiments, canary stages, and regional waves each produce release evidence, yet a candidate that passes offline accuracy on one dataset, passes latency benchmarks on a lighter synthetic load profile, and enters an online A/B test without a tested rollback target remains unverified as a whole. Those checks never evaluated the same release state. Evidence from different stages is useful only when it refers to the same candidate and decision. An **evaluation contract**\index{Evaluation contract!definition} is the versioned release record that binds a model and its dependencies to the workload, metrics, statistical design, acceptance thresholds, rollback conditions, and accountable owners. This record is the subject of the evaluation contract principle (\ref{pri-evaluation-contract}), one of the fleet-in-production principles listed in the opener to this part of the book. It holds that a fleet release decision is valid only when all of its evidence refers to one versioned contract. The record therefore becomes the unit of validity for everything this chapter has built, from registry versions and feature contracts to rollout stages and experiment statistics. @Tbl-ops-scale-evaluation-contract assembles that record across five evidence planes.

edges.label: sets acceptance criteria for

edges.explanation: An assurance case ties deployment claims to evidence and controls under a declared intended use.
edges.conditions: Evidence is bounded by the tested population, environment, and material-change policy.

evidence.quote: Acceptance is deliberately distributed, but promotion authority is not ambiguous. The model and domain owners accept predictive utility; the serving owner accepts capacity and reliability; specialist risk owners accept bounded robustness, fairness, privacy, and safety claims. A named release authority promotes only when all required sign-offs refer to the same artifact. The platform automates gates and preserves evidence, but it cannot choose the product objective or waive a failed assurance claim.

edges.label: supplies evidence to

edges.explanation: No single detector or robust objective covers all poisoning pathways.
edges.conditions: Controls must be selected for attacker access, contamination assumptions, and acceptable false positives.

evidence.quote:
1. **Ingress controls** establish provenance and access limits, dictating which sources may contribute or modify data.
2. **Anomaly detection and sanitization** inspect candidate records before training and filter suspicious submissions.
3. **Robust training objectives** reduce the weight that extreme residuals receive for poisoned samples that evade ingestion filtering, although they do not by themselves bound parameter updates.
4. **Post-training checks** test the trained model's behavior on the poisoning objectives that aggregate accuracy hides before the model is released.

edges.label: is addressed in layers by

edges.explanation: Repeated releases compose privacy loss under the stated accounting method.
edges.conditions: State the protected unit, sampling assumptions, mechanism, and composition rule.

evidence.quote: Privacy accounting depends on three primary composition tools. Simple composition\index{Differential privacy!simple composition} bounds the cumulative privacy loss of $\ComposedMechanismCount$ pure-DP mechanisms with bounds $\PrivacyBudget_i$ by $\sum \PrivacyBudget_i$; for approximate DP, their additive slack parameters also accumulate. In suitable parameter regimes, advanced composition\index{Differential privacy!advanced composition} improves the bound using square-root and linear terms while allocating additional slack in the probability inequality. For iterative mechanisms like DP-SGD, the moments accountant and Rényi differential privacy\index{Differential privacy!Rényi differential privacy}\index{Rényi differential privacy!composition tracking} developed next track the loss across steps before converting it to an explicit $(\PrivacyBudget, \PrivacyAdditiveSlack)$ guarantee, and no accountant is uniformly tighter than every alternative. Organizations must maintain a privacy accounting log for the protected population and halt or redesign further data-dependent releases when the allocated bound would be exceeded.

edges.label: is accounted through

edges.explanation: A shifted operational distribution may invalidate reference performance evidence and trigger evaluation.
edges.conditions: Detected input drift is evidence to investigate; it does not alone prove predictive degradation.

evidence.quote: Invalidation is the return path through the contract. Drift beyond the evaluated population, a feature or label-definition change, exhausted latency headroom, a statistically supported guardrail regression, or a material governance change sends the candidate back to the owning gate. Thresholds and rollback targets are fixed before exposure so an apparent primary-metric gain cannot redefine success after the result is known. Reproducibility requires retaining the inputs to that decision, not merely its verdict: the dataset and traffic snapshot, model and code versions, environment and hardware envelope, random seeds, assignment and sampling rules, sufficient statistics or permitted logs, approvals, and the exact rollback artifact.

edges.label: can invalidate evidence for

edges.explanation: Abstained requests may be routed to a stronger model or human review; their rate determines the fallback capacity required.
edges.conditions: Measure the risk-coverage operating point, route mix, service time, and response deadline; fallback capacity does not itself establish prediction validity.

evidence.quote: Set size or interval width supplies an operational load signal. Larger outputs convey less specific predictions and can trigger abstention, a stronger model, or human review, so their tail distribution determines fallback capacity just as the risk-coverage curve determines rejected traffic. The target coverage is therefore not free: increasing it usually widens sets, raises review demand, or reduces the fraction of requests on which the system can act automatically.

edges.label: creates demand for

edges.explanation: Moving eligible work to lower-carbon times or regions can reduce attributed operational emissions.
edges.conditions: Include transfer, added runtime, deadlines, capacity, and the selected average or marginal carbon signal.

evidence.quote: Carbon intensity varies across geographic locations and time periods, creating optimization opportunities. Temporal scheduling can reduce emissions when deadline-tolerant workloads are shifted toward lower-carbon hours or regions, with the realized gain depending on workload flexibility, grid mix, and whether the scheduler uses average or marginal emissions [@patterson2022; @radovanovic2021carbonaware]. **Carbon-aware scheduling**\index{Carbon-aware scheduling!definition} automates that shift, moving flexible, nonurgent work toward times and regions with lower carbon intensity while respecting its deadline and the available capacity.

edges.label: can reduce

edges.explanation: Cleaner operating electricity does not remove hardware-manufacturing emissions from the lifecycle account.
edges.conditions: Compare designs under matched lifecycle allocation and service functional units.

evidence.quote:
1.  **Significance**: Training GPT-3 consumed approximately `{python} Gpt3HouseholdEnergyAnchor.gpt3_training_mwh_str` of energy [@li2020estimating], equivalent to roughly `{python} Gpt3HouseholdEnergyAnchor.gpt3_household_years_str` US household-years of electricity. The same lifecycle logic applies after training: pretrained models can often be adapted with far less work than training from scratch, and high-volume inference can eventually dominate total energy. Sustainable AI therefore tracks both one-time training runs and recurring serving workloads rather than treating model training as the whole footprint.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike corporate sustainability reporting (which aggregates energy usage into annual CO~2~ disclosures), sustainable AI engineering operates at the individual workload level. It selects hardware by FLOP/s per watt, schedules training during periods of high renewable availability, and chooses model architectures that minimize inference FLOPs rather than maximizing accuracy alone.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that switching to renewable energy solves the sustainability problem. For hardware-intensive ML, embodied carbon (the carbon emitted manufacturing the chips, servers, and cooling equipment before they ever run a training job) can rival operational carbon on clean grids or at low utilization. For battery-powered consumer devices, manufacturing can account for most of the lifecycle footprint [@gupta2022chasing]. Hardware longevity and utilization rate are therefore as important as energy source.

edges.label: remains after reducing

edges.explanation: Rack power is an instantaneous operating constraint; accumulated energy also depends on how long equipment runs.
edges.conditions: Integrate the measured power profile over time using the same equipment and facility boundary.

evidence.quote: The two limits obey different arithmetic (@fig-energy-wall). The power limit is instantaneous. A facility cannot draw more than its grid feed ($\FacilityPower\le \GridFeedCapacity$), which caps the number of servers active at once ($\PoweredServerCount\le \InformationTechnologyPower/ \ServerPower$) regardless of how long a job runs. The energy account is cumulative, integrating average power over wall-clock time to give run energy ($\TotalEnergy = \AveragePower\times \JobDuration$). Exceeding electrical or thermal capacity can force power limiting, throttling, or protective shutdown. Cumulative energy instead enters the electricity and emissions accounts, which also depend on tariffs and the applicable grid emissions factors.

edges.label: caps instantaneous power underlying

edges.explanation: Carbon-aware scheduling must use feasible physical placements and respect workload constraints.
edges.conditions: A lower-carbon site is not an option if its capacity, transfer path, or deadline contract is infeasible.

evidence.quote: Carbon intensity varies across geographic locations and time periods, creating optimization opportunities. Temporal scheduling can reduce emissions when deadline-tolerant workloads are shifted toward lower-carbon hours or regions, with the realized gain depending on workload flexibility, grid mix, and whether the scheduler uses average or marginal emissions [@patterson2022; @radovanovic2021carbonaware]. **Carbon-aware scheduling**\index{Carbon-aware scheduling!definition} automates that shift, moving flexible, nonurgent work toward times and regions with lower carbon intensity while respecting its deadline and the available capacity.

edges.label: is constrained by

edges.explanation: A deployment assurance case must name and justify its selected fairness requirements and evidence.
edges.conditions: Fairness criteria can conflict; no single metric establishes universal fairness.

evidence.quote: The lifecycle begins before model selection. Teams first define the intended use, prohibited uses, affected parties, operating environment, and decision consequences. They then identify harms and requirements, including subgroup performance, privacy, security, robustness, sustainability, human-oversight, and contestability obligations. Some controls are implemented locally; others are inherited from data providers, foundation-model vendors, cloud platforms, or downstream operators. Each inherited control needs an interface contract stating what the supplier guarantees, what evidence supports that guarantee, and which residual risks remain with the deploying organization.

edges.label: constrains

edges.explanation: Affected people need an operational route to contest outcomes and receive investigation or correction.
edges.conditions: An explanation alone is insufficient unless accountable owners can act on a challenge.

evidence.quote: Showing a rejected loan applicant a feature-attribution chart accomplishes nothing if the app offers no button to dispute an error in the credit file, no human reviewer with authority to overturn the rejection, and no immutable snapshot of the inputs that produced the score. Explanations serve accountability only when stakeholders can both understand and challenge system decisions. Transparency allows users, developers, auditors, and regulators to inspect how a system functions, assess its limitations, and identify sources of harm, but disclosure alone is not enough. In high-stakes domains, individuals and institutions need contestability\index{Contestability!system accountability}: the operational ability to interrogate, appeal, and reverse an automated decision.

evidence.quote: For differential privacy, governance consumes the mechanism and accounting established in @sec-security-privacy-differential-privacy-8c2b. Reviewers then evaluate that bound alongside utility, subgroup performance, and the private-data accesses outside training. Naming the method is insufficient evidence for approving the complete service.

evidence.quote: These four measures complement rather than replace one another. SLO goodput applies on top of MPG: a serving fleet that operates at a high fraction of its ideal hardware rate on average can still violate latency targets in the tail if batches are formed too aggressively. Similarly, statistical goodput evaluates progress per example rather than operations per second, so enlarging the global batch beyond the critical batch size can raise program goodput while reducing statistical goodput. Any quantitative efficiency claim must therefore state which goodput measure it reports, which denominator defines its boundary, and which time window it spans. The measurement contract of @sec-performance-engineering-measuring-goodput pins down the workload, boundary, and measurement window so that two goodput numbers can be compared fairly.

edges.conditions: Include facility overhead exactly once and specify average versus marginal attribution.

evidence.quote: The Fleet Law connects execution time to the fleet energy account. A step's energy is approximately its average fleet power times $\DistributedStepTime(\DeviceCount)$ (@eq-sustainable-ai-step-energy), so exposed communication and synchronization extend the interval over which the system draws power. Recovery adds further work outside successful steps. The C³ terms therefore matter to both performance and sustainability, although the power trace determines their energy cost. edges.explanation: The cache budget is the memory left after weights and other runtime allocations.
edges.conditions: Reserve runtime headroom and account for total cached tokens rather than request count alone.

evidence.quote: A replica's KV footprint is that cost multiplied by every token it holds, $\KvCacheMemory = \BatchSize \times \SequenceLength \times \KvCacheBytesPerToken$, so the largest admissible batch at context $\SequenceLength$ is the HBM left after weights and runtime allocations divided by $\SequenceLength \times \KvCacheBytesPerToken$. Each serving lever acts on a different factor. Grouped-query attention lowers $\KvHeadCount$, KV quantization lowers $\ElementStorageSize$, a shorter admitted context lowers $\SequenceLength$, and paging returns HBM lost to fragmentation without changing the per-token cost. The notebook below turns this budget into an explicit batch-size limit for a production node.

edges.label: bounds admission using

edges.explanation: Post-training checks evaluate attack-specific behavior before a model is released; clean aggregate accuracy alone cannot rule out targeted or backdoor poisoning.
edges.conditions: The checks cover only their stated poisoning threat models, target cohorts, and trigger assumptions; an unseen backdoor can evade them.

evidence.quote:
1. **Ingress controls** establish provenance and access limits, dictating which sources may contribute or modify data.
2. **Anomaly detection and sanitization** inspect candidate records before training and filter suspicious submissions.
3. **Robust training objectives** reduce the weight that extreme residuals receive for poisoned samples that evade ingestion filtering, although they do not by themselves bound parameter updates.
4. **Post-training checks** test the trained model's behavior on the poisoning objectives that aggregate accuracy hides before the model is released.

edges.label: requires checks before

edges.explanation: Fully sharded workers gather a module's parameter shards before computation needs full weights.
edges.conditions: This describes full parameter sharding; other ZeRO stages and resharding policies have different schedules.

evidence.quote: Ring achieves AllReduce's bandwidth-optimal cost while the simple full-message Tree model\index{Broadcast!tree topology} trades bandwidth for logarithmic latency [@patarasuk2009; @thakur2005]. AllReduce itself also decomposes into ReduceScatter\index{ReduceScatter!decomposition} followed by AllGather\index{AllGather!decomposition}. The decomposition is operational as well as mathematical, since Ring AllReduce's first phase is a ReduceScatter and its second phase is an AllGather. ReduceScatter performs arithmetic, so it does not invert AllGather despite reversing the direction of shard expansion. Full ZeRO-style sharding\index{ZeRO!parameter sharding} and PyTorch FSDP use the pair the same way, gathering parameter shards with AllGather before a module needs them and reducing gradients with ReduceScatter after backward so each rank retains only its shard for the optimizer step [@rajbhandari2020]. Sharding parameters, gradients, and optimizer state across workers reduces persistent model-state memory roughly by $\DeviceCount\times$, while temporary full-parameter buffers and prefetching determine peak memory. That memory saving is developed in @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-memoryefficient-data-parallelism-zero-fsdp-0e69; the communication it adds is priced in @sec-communication-fsdp-patterns.

edges.label: completes reconstruction with

edges.explanation: An FSDP parameter gather can overlap independent work only while its arrival still satisfies the layer dependency.
edges.conditions: Extra materialized parameters consume memory; the available compute window and actual transfer rate bound hidden time.

evidence.quote: Selecting the right collective algorithm at each invocation requires distinguishing transfer cost from dependency exposure. An FSDP AllGather is latency-sensitive\index{FSDP!AllGather latency sensitivity} in the scheduling sense, because a layer cannot compute until its full parameters arrive. Its transfer can nevertheless be bandwidth-bound when the parameter tensor is large. Prefetching can hide part of that gather, while a ReduceScatter can overlap with the remaining backward computation. Neither dependency alone selects Ring or Tree; message size, group size, topology, and the available overlap window jointly determine the useful schedule.

edges.label: can be prefetched for

edges.explanation: Release acceptance includes production-equivalent capacity and reliability evidence for the same candidate, workload, and thresholds. Serving SLO goodput is interpretable only under that fixed serving contract.
edges.conditions: The serving workload and latency targets must be those named by the release contract; training MPG cannot stand in for this evidence.

evidence.quote: Acceptance is deliberately distributed, but promotion authority is not ambiguous. The model and domain owners accept predictive utility; the serving owner accepts capacity and reliability; specialist risk owners accept bounded robustness, fairness, privacy, and safety claims. A named release authority promotes only when all required sign-offs refer to the same artifact. The platform automates gates and preserves evidence, but it cannot choose the product objective or waive a failed assurance claim.
